transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE); Raj Patel (CTO, Bluewave); Olivia Gomez (Platform Eng, Bluewave); Dr. Sara Lin (ML Lead); Noah Rivera (Security)

Auto-Summary: Kickoff to align on POC success criteria and harness integration. Focus on realistic traffic, streaming fallback, and security constraints for an on-prem/private pilot.

Topics: success criteria, workload sizing, streaming vs non-streaming, bench matrix, timeline, security artifacts.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with Liam who's our solutions engineer. quick check on who we have on the call?
[00:15] Raj: Raj here, CTO at Bluewave, Olivia and Sara are with me, and Noah is on for security.
[00:20] Olivia: hi all, yep
[00:22] Sara: hi
[00:24] Liam: cool thanks. goal for today is to land on a benchmark plan and the harness integration points, like which scripts you already have, streaming client behavior and what acceptance looks like.
[00:35] Raj: sounds good. to frame, we're evaluating Redwood to replace an internal inference layer for clinical summarization, must be sub-200ms p50 for short prompts and p95 under 600ms for our interactive UI, and throughput has to scale to approx 120 QPS peak sustained for one service. those are rough numbers.
[01:00] Maya: great that's super helpful. can you remind us about data residency and whether this will be private/VPC or hosted?
[01:15] Noah: key point is for production we need private VPC — no logs leaving zone without encryption and we have strict KMS requirements, HSM not required yet but would prefer bring-your-own-kms. also SOC2 and we do periodic audits.
[01:35] Liam: ok noted. for the POC are you open to Redwood hosted with dedicated capacity for initial benchmarks, then move to private? or do you want private from day one?
[01:50] Raj: we'd prefer private but we can do initial perf runs on Redwood hosted if we fog the data. We need to understand cold start behavior and KV cache warmup impact as that's critical for our latency tail.
[02:10] Sara: also want to validate hallucination/regression checks — but for this POC success criteria primary is latency and throughput, second is quality regression within our eval set.
[02:35] Maya: good, so success criteria: p50 <200ms, p95 <600ms for short prompts, throughput sustain 120 QPS with acceptable token cost, and model output quality within delta threshold on your evals. i'll put that in the matrix.
[02:55] Olivia: on scripts we have a couple formats: 1) production replay logs in JSON (session-based), 2) a set of 200 unit test prompts with expected outputs. we can provide those. question — what does your harness expect for streaming vs non-streaming?
[03:20] Liam: our harness supports two flows — streaming (chunked tokens over a persistent connection) and non-streaming (request/response). streaming reduces perceived latency for long generations but increases connection management complexity. we usually test both: microbench for p50 token latency and macro load for throughput.
[03:45] Raj: we also have a mixed mode where short prompts use non-streaming and long notes use streaming. we'd like the POC to show mixed-mode throughput and fallback behavior.
[04:00] Maya: ok we'll include mixed-mode scenarios. one question about auth: Olivia, what does your auth flow look like? SAML? API keys?
[04:12] Olivia: SAML for UI, but for service-to-service we use mTLS and short-lived API tokens issued by our auth service. we'll share the auth handshake and sample token endpoint.
[04:25] Liam: that's fine. the adapter we provide will include mTLS support and a sample token refresher. for the harness adapter we can give a python example and a Go one. which do you prefer?
[04:42] Olivia: python first please.
[04:45] Maya: noted. next, workload sizing — can you describe the request size distribution? average tokens per request?
[04:55] Sara: average is 45 tokens, median 28, long tail up to 600 tokens for full patient notes. 70% short prompts, 30% long-form.
[05:15] Liam: that distribution matters a lot for KV cache and batching. for short prompts we optimize for low-latency paths and small batch sizes, for long-form we lean on streaming and larger batch windows.
[05:35] Raj: how do you simulate concurrency? do you replay sessions to maintain KV cache per session?
[05:45] Liam: yes we recommend session-aware replay — maintain KV per conversation id so cache warmup is realistic. the harness can replay with session affinity. if you can't provide session ids, we can synthetic ones but results differ.
[06:05] Olivia: we can add session ids to logs.
[06:10] Maya: excellent. the benchmark matrix we'll propose will include: short prompt microbench (p50/p95), long prompt streaming latency, mixed-mode throughput sustained for 30 minutes at peak profile, cold-start and warm-up runs, token cost metrics, and a quality regression run using your 200 tests.
[06:40] Raj: what's your definition of cold start here? container spin-up vs kernel warmup?
[06:48] Liam: two things: model cold start (container or process spin-up) and KV cold (no cache). we'll run both: 1) cold process then steady state, 2) warm process with empty KV and measure warmup curve.
[07:05] Noah: from security side we need audit logs for every inference call and proof we can rotate keys without downtime. what's typical log retention and can you hook to our SIEM?
[07:20] Maya: Redwood Console can stream audit logs to your ingestion (S3/Kinesis/etc) and we support SIEM integrations. retention is configurable, default 90 days but enterprise can extend. key rotation we support KMS integrations and we can do zero-downtime rotation with staged keys — Liam can follow up on the runbook.
[07:45] Liam: yep i'll send the key rotation runbook.
[07:50] Raj: good. now about measurement noise — how do you ensure the harness results are reproducible?
[07:58] Liam: we recommend 3 runs for each scenario, fixed seed for deterministic model outputs when possible, and controlling background load on the host. bootstrap with KV warmup script to reach steady-state. we capture token-level timings and request tracer IDs so we can map tails to client events.
[08:20] Sara: about deterministic seeds, we use a regen test tolerance because some models are non-deterministic. can you do delta-based quality checks?
[08:28] Maya: yes we support tolerance thresholds and per-prompt scoring.
[08:32] Raj: timeline question: how long to get a harness adapter in our infra and run first smoke tests?
[08:38] Liam: with the artifacts you promised (traffic traces + auth details) we can deliver an adapter skeleton in 3 business days, smoke tests in 1-2 days after that, and a full benchmark run in ~7 days after adapter stabilization. so roughly 2 weeks to initial pilot if everything aligns.
[08:58] Olivia: sounds reasonable. are there special infra requirements? GPUs?
[09:05] Liam: depends on model size. for the POC we can run on Redwood hosted with suitable GPU profile — we'll include recommended instance types in the matrix. for private on-prem you'll need GPU nodes with CUDA and the inference runtime; we'll provide an install script.
[09:25] Raj: one more: how do you handle fallback when capacity is exhausted? we want graceful degradation, not hard errors.
[09:33] Maya: Redwood routing supports fallback policies; we can define a tiered model fallback (smaller quantized variant) and queueing to keep requests alive within SLA. we'll include those thresholds in the runbook.
[09:50] Noah: also can you show logs that redact PHI? since we're in healthcare that's critical.
[09:58] Liam: yes we can configure PII/PHI redaction in the logging pipeline and only export aggregated metrics to hosted telemetry. full trace logs can remain within your VPC.
[10:12] Sara: on quality testing, can you run our evaluation harness (python pytest style) against model outputs as part of the bench?
[10:20] Liam: absolutely. we can integrate your eval harness into the pipeline so after each run we produce a quality report with per-prompt scores and regression flags.
[10:30] Maya: OK let's capture concrete acceptance criteria now. p50 <200ms short prompt; p95 <600ms short prompt; sustained 120 QPS mixed-profile for 30 minutes with <2% error rate; quality delta on upstream eval less than X (we'll let you define X). any objections?
[10:50] Raj: that works, but on p95 we may tolerate 700ms if token cost is significantly lower — we need a cost/latency tradeoff in the matrix.
[11:02] Maya: we will add a cost column and include quantized model variants.
[11:08] Olivia: for the harness we need example client instrumentation — traces, request ids, and a way to map session tokens back to replay logs.
[11:18] Liam: adapter will emit request_id and session_id and accept session-affinity param. we'll include a mapping guide in the README.
[11:28] Sara: about streaming fallback — if streaming connection drops mid-generation, does the harness retry or fall back to non-streaming?
[11:38] Liam: by default we attempt a resumable token stream when supported; otherwise we fall back to a non-streamed regeneration. the harness can simulate network jitter and we can capture behavior.
[11:55] Raj: can you run a test that intentionally drops 5% of streaming connections to measure user-perceived latency?
[12:02] Maya: yes we'll add a fault-injection scenario.
[12:08] Noah: what about encryption in transit: mTLS is fine but we also need to ensure server-side KMS usage for model keys?
[12:18] Liam: for keys we support customer-managed KMS, we store only encrypted blobs and we never persist raw keys. detailed architecture doc will be shared.
[12:30] Maya: let's talk deliverables — we'll produce a benchmark matrix CSV, harness adapter repo link, runbook for key rotation and fallback, and initial results. we'll also include recommended instance specs and estimated token cost for the pilot.
[12:48] Olivia: can we get an estimate of token cost for 120 QPS at your recommended model?
[12:55] Maya: we'll populate an estimated monthly cost with a couple model options (base vs quantized) in the matrix.
[13:05] Raj: final question — do you support traffic mirroring so we can shadow-prod traffic into the bench?
[13:12] Liam: yes traffic mirroring is supported — we recommend a small sample first not full production to avoid accidental writes. we can show a mirroring playbook.
[13:25] Maya: ok great. wrapping up — recapping next steps: Redwood to send the benchmark matrix and adapter README by 10/15; Bluewave to share traffic traces and auth details by 10/18; security review 10/20; pilot start week of 10/25.
[13:45] Raj: yeah that timeline works for us. thanks everyone.
[13:50] Olivia: thanks
[13:52] Sara: thanks
[13:53] Noah: thanks
[13:54] Maya: bye all
